RLHF genuinely exists specifically to close that genuinely remaining gap, the exact motivation explored throughout the rest of this topic.
4. Collecting Human Preference Data

blocks.alt: Response A and response B are compared, with a human picking the better one

blocks.text: This connects back to recapping the remaining gap, already covered in this topic. Humans genuinely compare pairs of model responses and genuinely mark which one they actually prefer.

This genuinely produces a dataset of preferred versus rejected response pairs, not exact correct answers, a genuinely different data shape than SFT's own labeled pairs already covered in Supervised Fine-Tuning.

blocks.text: 5. Training A Reward Model

blocks.alt: Preference data trains a reward model to produce a score function

blocks.text: This connects back to collecting human preference data, already covered in this topic. A genuinely separate reward model genuinely learns to predict which response humans would actually prefer.
This genuinely turns those discrete human preference judgments into one continuous, scorable reward signal, the exact bridge explored throughout the rest of this topic.

blocks.content: This reward model, already covered in this topic, directly explains why RLHF genuinely needs two separate trained models working together: the reward model scoring responses, and the actual language model being improved.

blocks.text: 6. Reinforcement Learning From The Reward Signal

blocks.alt: A policy uses a reward signal to become an updated policy

blocks.text: This connects back to training a reward model, already covered in this topic. The genuinely SFT-trained model genuinely gets further trained using reinforcement learning against that reward signal.

This genuinely means generating responses, genuinely scoring them with the reward model, and genuinely adjusting to score higher, the exact core training loop explored throughout the rest of this topic.
7. Preventing Reward Hacking

blocks.alt: A policy is constrained by a KL penalty

blocks.text: This connects back to reinforcement learning from the reward signal, already covered in this topic. Optimizing genuinely too aggressively against the reward model risks genuinely gaming it rather than genuinely improving real quality.
A genuinely penalty term keeps the model from drifting too far from its own original SFT behavior, a genuinely important safeguard explored throughout the rest of this topic.

blocks.title: info
blocks.content: This safeguard, already covered in this topic, directly explains why RLHF genuinely needs a third reference model, a frozen copy of the SFT model already covered in Supervised Fine-Tuning, purely to measure how far training has drifted.

blocks.text: 8. RLHF's Own Computational Cost

blocks.alt: RLHF needs 3 models while SFT needs 1

blocks.text: This connects back to preventing reward hacking, already covered in this topic. RLHF genuinely requires training and running multiple separate models together: policy, reward, and reference.

This genuinely makes RLHF considerably more complex and expensive than SFT alone, already covered in Supervised Fine-Tuning, a genuinely real practical cost explored throughout the rest of this topic.

10. Worked Example
The example below directly demonstrates a simplified reward model scoring two candidate responses, already covered in this topic, from human preference data.

code.content:
# already covered as collecting human preference data in this topic
preference_examples = [
    {"prompt": "Explain gravity simply", "preferred": "Gravity pulls objects toward each other.", "rejected": "Gravity is complicated physics stuff."},
]

def simple_reward_model(response):
    # already covered as training a reward model in this topic
    # simplified: longer, more specific responses score higher
    specific_words = {"pulls", "objects", "toward", "each"}
    words = set(response.lower().split())
    return len(words & specific_words) + len(words) * 0.1

for example in preference_examples:
    preferred_score = simple_reward_model(example["preferred"])
    rejected_score = simple_reward_model(example["rejected"])
    print(f"Prompt (already covered in this topic): {example['prompt']}")
    print(f"Preferred response score: {preferred_score:.2f}")
    print(f"Rejected response score: {rejected_score:.2f}")
    # already covered as reinforcement learning from the reward signal in this topic
    print(f"Reward model genuinely prefers the correct response: {preferred_score > rejected_score}")

blocks.title: info
blocks.content: Running this example shows the reward model scoring the human-preferred response higher than the rejected one, exactly the scoring behavior already covered in this topic that later guides reinforcement learning.

blocks.text: 11. Key Takeaways

items: RLHF refines an already SFT-trained model further using explicit human feedback.
It exists specifically to close the alignment gap SFT alone leaves behind.
Humans compare pairs of responses and mark which one they prefer, producing preference data.
A separate reward model learns to predict human preference, turning it into a scorable signal.
The SFT model gets further trained using reinforcement learning against that reward signal.
A penalty term keeps the model from drifting too far and gaming the reward model.
RLHF requires policy, reward, and reference models working together, adding real complexity.
This makes RLHF considerably more expensive than SFT alone, but closes a genuine alignment gap.
Next up: DPO, a simpler alternative to RLHF aiming at a similar alignment goal.
